newsitem.title: FRANCE: TWA missile "evidence" long worldwide on Internet.
newsitem.headline: TWA missile "evidence" long worldwide on Internet.

text.p: Evidence cited by former White House adviser Pierre Salinger on Friday for his charge that a U.S. Navy missile accidentally shot down a TWA airliner last July has been circulating freely worldwide on the Internet.
Salinger told French television the document saying that the Boeing 747 with 230 people aboard was downed in a missile test off New York had been on the Internet computer network for two months.
He also acknowledged on French television channel TF1 that he had got the document, which he initially said came from a U.S. secret service agent, second-hand from an unnamed Frenchman.

"Actually, I found out last night that it had been on Internet for two months," Salinger, the press spokesman for the late president John F. Kennedy and later Paris bureau chief for the U.S. television network ABC, told TF1 in French.
The document, which Salinger carried in his hand as he posed for photographers, bore wide similarities, including several identical paragraphs, with another posted on the Internet.
A casual Internet search turned up a myriad of documents discussing the so-called "missile theory", with several offering scenarios similar to that put forward by Salinger.
He said his document showed that the Navy had conducted the test at an altitude of 13,000 feet (3,950 metres) in the belief that all aircraft in the area were flying at 21,000 feet (6,400 metres).

The airport control tower, in "a tragic error", failed to inform the Navy that Trans World Airlines flight 800 had taken off late from New York because of heavy traffic and was flying lower than expected to stay clear of another aircraft, he said.

After saying initially he had been given the document in Paris by a U.S. secret service agent, Salinger later said he received it five weeks ago "from a Frenchman involved in various government things who had met a man from the U.S. Secret Service who had written a paper on what happened in the TWA crash".
Salinger, 71, nevertheless said he stood by the document's allegations. He later left his hotel in the Mediterranean resort of Cannes for an undisclosed destination.
The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the U.S. Defence Department both insisted there was no evidence that a missile was involved in the crash.
The U.S. Navy said it had no weapons in the area at the time that could have shot down the airliner, and federal investigators had already found the possibility "without merit".

A missile, a bomb or a mechanical fault have all been suggested as possible causes for the crash of the Paris-bound flight, which occurred just days before the opening of the 1996 Olympic Games in Atlanta.
There has been no verdict yet in the official probe.

Salinger said he was not surprised by the denials and offered to show the FBI his document, suggesting the evidence in his possession might have been withheld to avoid embarrassing President Bill Clinton before Tuesday's presidential election.
"Now it will be interesting to see since the election is three days ago whether there will be a change in the way they are doing the investigation," he told Reuters earlier in the day.
Salinger said he had decided to make his allegations after the French weekly Paris Match published a "very important" picture and "no one in the United States looked at this for one second".
The picture, said to have been taken during a party on Long Island at the time of the crash, appeared to show a missile-like object streaking through the sky.
Salinger said he had passed on his information to ABC, which told him: "Now is not the time."

In Paris, a lawyer for the relatives of the 45 French citizens killed on board the airliner said he had asked investigating magistrate Chantal Perdrix to question Salinger and have the Paris Match picture scrutinised by police experts.
A statement from families of the victims later said Perdrix had agreed to seek to question Salinger and ask him to show the document on which he based his accusations.
Perdrix has opened a probe into the crash to determine whether manslaughter or murder charges are warranted.

Investigators have recovered most of the wreckage but are still dredging the seabed off Long Island for evidence to explain the crash. They have established that a fuel tank exploded but not what set off the blast.
